tip: 'geçen yaz' = last summer. 'geçen' (passing) marks the previous one: 'geçen hafta' (last week), 'geçen yıl' (last year).
'geçeriz' uses the -er ending for a hopeful outcome after 'inşallah' (hopefully). This -er form also covers likely future events.
'dükkanda' = 'dükkan' + da (in the shop). Add -da or -de to a noun for in, at, or on.
'oturup' links two verbs: 'oturup' then 'okumayı' (sitting and reading). The -ip ending means and then, borrowing the last verb's tense.
'yazmakta' = in writing: 'yazmak' (to write) plus -ta (at). 'zorlanıyorum' joins it to mean I struggle at doing it.
'içmedim' is the negative past of 'içtim': iç + me + dim (I did not drink). The -me before -dim flips it to negative.
'bakalım' = let's look. The -alım or -elim ending on a verb makes a let's suggestion: 'gidelim', 'bakalım'.
'çalışmayacağız' ends in ğ, not k: the k of the future -acak softens to ğ before the vowel ending -ız.
'okumuyorsun' hides the negative: before -yor the -ma of 'okuma' narrows to -mu, so oku + mu + yor + sun.
'mutfaktan' means from the kitchen: the from ending is -tan after a voiceless k, and -dan after voiced sounds.
'şiir' carries no object ending here: an unmarked object means poetry in general, not one specific poem.
'geldik' means we came: -di marks a past action you witnessed, and the final -k is the we ending.
'görebilir miyim' means may I see: the -ebil inside 'görebilir' marks can or be able to do something.
Turkish needs no verb for is there: 'et var mı' literally asks meat there-is?, using 'var' plus the question word 'mı'.
'hem ... hem de' means both ... and: it brackets the two actions, 'hem çalışıyorum hem de gidiyorum'.
'plaja' means to the beach: adding -a to 'plaj' marks motion toward something. Front-vowel words take -e instead.
'arabalarını' stacks endings: araba + lar (plural) + ı (their) + the object ending, meaning their cars as a definite object.
'varacaksınız' = var + acak + sınız, you will arrive: future uses -acak after back vowels, -ecek after front ones.
'söndürmeye çalışıyor' means trying to put out: the verb takes -meye (to) before 'çalışmak', to try.
'kedinin tüyleri' means the cat's fur: 'kedi' takes -nin (of the cat) and 'tüy' takes -leri (its).
'dikkat et' is the informal command take care: the bare verb stem alone tells one person to do something.
'geçmiş' uses -mış, the reported past: it frames students passed as hearsay or inference, not something you personally saw.
'yerine' follows the noun to mean instead of it: 'restoran yerine' = instead of a restaurant.
'kapandığını' turns a whole clause into an object: -dığı plus the object ending lets you say know what time it closed.
'asırdır' adds -dır meaning for: 'çeyrek asırdır' = for a quarter century, marking how long the action has gone on.
'ailece' means as a family: adding -ce to 'aile' makes an adverb, the whole group doing it together.
'sabırla' means patiently: the -la ending (with) turns the noun 'sabır' (patience) into a manner adverb.
'değil mi' is the tag isn't it: 'değil' means not, so 'güzel değil mi' asks nice, no?, inviting agreement.
'dolaşır' and 'izler' take the -r or -ir ending: this general tense states habits and routines, not an action happening right now.
'arasında' means between and follows its nouns: 'okul ile ev arasında' = between school and home, position words come last.
